title: Lab 02 — Standard Errors and Randomization Tests
text:
Load libraries
Load tidyverse library

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(here) # resolves files from the project root regardless of where qmd lives

here() starts at /mnt/data1/documents/ISU/RProjects/STAT5101




Writing functions in R
Load data (user header=TRUE)

creativity <- read.csv(here("data/creativity.csv"), header = TRUE)
head(creativity)

  treatment score
1 intrinsic  12.0
2 intrinsic  12.0
3 intrinsic  12.9
4 intrinsic  13.6
5 intrinsic  16.6
6 intrinsic  17.2


Define function for computing the standard error

se <- function(x) {
    s <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    n <- sum(!is.na(x))
    s / sqrt(n)
}

Calculate standard error for all 47 observation scores (just the score column)

se(creativity$score)

[1] 0.7653046


Using tidyverse, summarize the standard error (a different way to calculate)

creativity |>
    summarize(
        se = se(score)
    )

         se
1 0.7653046


Group by treatment and compute the standard error by treatment group

creativity |>
    group_by(treatment) |>
    summarize(
        se = se(score)
    )

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  treatment    se
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 extrinsic 1.10 
2 intrinsic 0.906




Randomization Tests
First set seed for reproducibility

set.seed(5101)

Calculate the observed difference in mean score (observed means as documented in creativity.csv)

observed_diff <- creativity |>
    group_by(treatment) |>
    summarize(mean_score = mean(score)) |>
    summarize(diff = diff(mean_score)) |>
    pull(diff)

observed_diff

[1] 4.100725


Run randomization (basically, simulate what else, other than what was recorded in the csv, could have been observed at random)

nsim <- 10000
simulated_diffs <- replicate(nsim, {
    # Everthing in {} is evaluated as if it was a function (this is like a lambda)
    creativity |>
        # generate a random treatment value
        mutate(shuffled = sample(treatment)) |>
        # group by the random treatment value
        group_by(shuffled) |>
        # Calculate the mean and diff like before
        summarize(mean_score = mean(score)) |>
        summarize(diff = diff(mean_score)) |>
        # pull the difference
        pull(diff)
})
head(simulated_diffs)

[1]  2.7043478  1.4356884  0.9077899 -1.6465580  0.8141304  1.8614130


Calculate the p-value

p_value <- (1 + sum(abs(simulated_diffs) >= abs(observed_diff))) / (nsim + 1)
p_value

[1] 0.00489951


Explanation of p-value calculation: The p-value is the number of observations with a value equal to or more extreme (>=) than the observed value divided by the number of observations. This would translate to:
sum(abs(simulated_diffs) >= abs(simulated_diff)) / nsim
But, this results in a 0 p-value if by chance the observed_diff was an extreme value itself and none of the simulated values were equal or larger resulting in 0 / nsim = 0, which is an impossible p-value.
By adding 1 to both the numerator and denominator, essentially, we are including the observed_diff in the calculation. Since observed_diff is equal to itself, it is valid to include it as a count in the numerator and increment the denominator by 1 as if we performed 10001 simulations instead of 10000.


Self Assessment
Read in the tomato data, tomato.csv

tomato <- read.csv(here("data/tomato.csv"), header = TRUE)
head(tomato)

  treatment yield
1         a  0.39
2         b  0.44
3         a  1.83
4         a  5.66
5         b  0.33
6         a  8.06



(a) Draw side-by-side box plots of the yield for each fertilizer

ggplot(data = tomato, mapping=aes(x = treatment, y = yield)) +
    geom_boxplot()










(b) Estimate the difference in mean yield between the two fertilizers (a-b)

observed_diff = tomato |>
    group_by(treatment) |>
    summarize(mean_yield = mean(yield)) |>
    summarize(diff = diff(mean_yield)) |>
    pull(diff)
observed_diff

[1] -6.531429




(c) Estimate the difference in median yield

tomato |>
    group_by(treatment) |>
    summarize(median_yield = median(yield)) |>
    summarize(diff = diff(median_yield)) |>
    pull(diff)

[1] -4.64




(d) Use a randomization test to test the null hypothesis of no effect of the fertilizer on mean yield. Report the two-sided p-value
Run randomization test and collect simulated diffs

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(5101)

# We have already calculated the observed diff above
# Run randomization test

nsim <- 10000
simulated_diffs <- replicate(nsim, {
    tomato |>
        mutate(shuffled = sample(treatment)) |>
        group_by(shuffled) |>
        summarize(mean_yield = mean(yield)) |>
        summarize(diff = diff(mean_yield)) |>
        pull(diff)
})
head(simulated_diffs)

[1]  2.305714 -1.914286  4.940000  2.337143 -1.040000 -3.597143


Calculate p-value

p_value = (1 + sum(abs(simulated_diffs) >= abs(observed_diff))) / (nsim + 1)
p_value

[1] 0.03659634


Comments: Treatment a (the proposed better fertilizer) produced a mean yield 6.53 pounds higher than treatment b (p = 0.037). This provides moderate evidence against the null hypothesis of no fertilizer effect — a difference this large would occur by chance alone only about 3.7% of the time under random assignment. Since the 7 plants per group were randomly assigned to treatments, a causal conclusion is justified: the better fertilizer caused higher yield in this experiment. However, since the 14 plants were not randomly selected from any broader population, we cannot generalize beyond these particular plants.

2. Introduction to Computing

Basics
Load necessary packages

library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

library(ggplot2)

Read CSV

creativity <- read.csv("../data/creativity.csv")
names(creativity)

[1] "treatment" "score"    


Print the first 6 (default) observations

head(creativity)

  treatment score
1 intrinsic  12.0
2 intrinsic  12.0
3 intrinsic  12.9
4 intrinsic  13.6
5 intrinsic  16.6

Quick six-number summary of numerical column score

summary(creativity$score)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.

summarize(creativity)

data frame with 0 columns and 1 row




Using the “pipe” operator |>

creativity |>

  treatment score

Select columns from a data frame

creativity |>

    head()

  score
1  12.0
2  12.0
3  12.9

Return six-number summary on the score column

creativity |>
    pull(score) |> # pull extracts a vector of the column values
    summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   5.00   14.90   18.70   17.88   21.25   29.70 


Return the mean of the score column

creativity |>
    pull(score) |>
    mean()

[1] 17.8766


Return mean using summarize:

creativity |>
    summarize(
        meanScore = mean(score)
    )

  meanScore
1   17.8766


Summarize many expressions

creativity |>
    summarize(
        meanScore = mean(score),
        medianScore = median(score),
        sdScore = sd(score)
    )

  meanScore medianScore  sdScore
1   17.8766        18.7 5.246664


Calculate summaries by treatment group

creativity |>
    group_by(treatment) |>
    summarize(
        meanScore = mean(score),
        medianScore = median(score),
        sdScore = sd(score)
    )

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  treatment meanScore medianScore sdScore
  <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 extrinsic      15.8        17.2    5.29
2 intrinsic      19.9        20.4    4.44




Plotting Data
Create a dot plot

Center all dots on x-axis value 1
y is the score variable
binaxis is the axis to bin along, using y here
stackdir specifies direction in which dots are stacked


ggplot(data = creativity, mapping = aes(x = 1, y = score)) +
    geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")








Create dot plots by treatment group

Use the treatment column in the x-axis


ggplot(data = creativity, mapping = aes(x = treatment, y = score)) +
    geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")








Avoid redundancy by building a template and adding different geom layers to the template

Create a template


creativity_setup1 <- ggplot(data = creativity, mapping = aes(x = score))


Add geom layer - histogram


creativity_setup1 + geom_histogram()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.










Add geom layer box_plot


creativity_setup1 + geom_boxplot()









Flip the box plot x and y axes


creativity_setup1 + 
    coord_flip() +
    geom_boxplot()








Work with treatment group

creativity_setup2 <- ggplot(data = creativity, mapping = aes(x = treatment, y = score))


Draw box plot per treatment group


creativity_setup2 + geom_boxplot()









Change theme to classic theme and redraw the same box plot


creativity_setup2 + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    theme_classic()








Specify different colors to visually separate groups

Create the template


creativity_setup3 <- ggplot(
    data = creativity, 
    mapping = aes(
        x = score,
        fill = treatment,
        color = treatment
    )
)


Draw histogram


creativity_setup3 + 
    geom_histogram(position = "dodge")

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.










Change color scale


creativity_setup3 +
    scale_color_grey() + 
    scale_fill_grey() +
    geom_histogram(position = "dodge")

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









Save the last plot

ggsave("figure.png")

Saving 7 x 5 in image
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.


Save a plot for HW1 submission:

creativity_setup2 + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    theme_classic()







ggsave("creativity_boxplot.png", width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)



Self-Assessment
Read tomato.csv

tomato_df <- read.csv("../data/tomato.csv")
names(tomato_df)

[1] "treatment" "yield"    


View the first 6 records

head(tomato_df)

Draw side-by-side box plots of each yield for each of the two fertilizers

ggplot(data = tomato_df, mapping = aes(x = treatment, y = yield)) +
    geom_boxplot() +

Estimate the difference in mean yield between the two fertilizers (a - b). Include units.

mean_a = tomato_df |> filter(treatment == "a") |> pull(yield) |> mean()
mean_b = tomato_df |> filter(treatment == "b") |> pull(yield) |> mean()

title: HW 02 — Randomization Tests
text:
Load Libraries

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(here)

here() starts at /mnt/data1/documents/ISU/RProjects/STAT5101




Problem 1
Problem 1 (Elderly hospitalization): You are conducting a study on hospital utilization among elderly residents in a small Iowa town. The focus is on the number of days each individual spent as an inpatient at the local hospital during 2023. To collect data, you begin with a complete list of all elderly residents in the town and then randomly select eleven individuals. For each of these residents, you record the total number of inpatient hospital days in 2023. The data are: 12, 3, 0, 0, 0, 4, 6, 7, 32, 14, 10. The data are also provided, for your convenience, in the file hospital.csv.

hospital <- read.csv(here("data/hospital.csv"))
hospital

   days
1    12
2     3
3     0
4     0
5     0
6     4
7     6
8     7
9    34
10   14
11   10



(a) Calculate and report the mean of these data

mean(hospital$days)

[1] 8.181818




(b) Calculate and report the median of these data

median(hospital$days)

[1] 6




(c) Calculate and report the standard deviation of these data

sd(hospital$days)

[1] 9.847012


For the next two parts, assume that patterns of hospitalization in 2026 will be the same as those in 2023. Also ignore the potential increase in hospitalization with age.


(d) Answer to grandmother’s question
Imagine that your grandmother is an elderly resident of this small town. She hears about your work and asks you “how many days am I likely to be in hospitalized in 2026?” What number would you tell her? Briefly explain your choice.
Answer: Since we have an outlier with 34 days, the mean is pulled towards it and is a little misleading. In this case, the median is a better answer since it is not affected by the outlier. So the answer is - Probably around 6 days but there is considerable variation.


(e) Answer to hospital administrator’s question
Imagine that the administrator of the only hospital in town asks you: “Can you estimate the total number of person-days that the elderly of this town will be in the hospital in 2026?” There are predicted to be 605 elderly residents of the town in 2026. What number would you tell her? Briefly explain your choice.
Answer: Person-Days are calculated using the mean. The median is not a right choice because its simply the midpoint. For sums and totals, mean is a better choice. Total Person-Days for 605 elderly residents would be 605 * 8.18 ~= 4949. So, assuming that 2026 hospitalization patterns are the same as 2023, which means we can use the same mean value, the answer to the hospital administrator’s question is 4949 days.



Problem 2
Problem 2 (Radon levels): The file radon.txt contains measurements from a simple random sample of 42 owner-occupied homes in Ramsey County, Minnesota. Each number shows the level of radon gas (in pCi/L) found in that home. Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can build up indoors and may pose health risks, so studying its levels helps us understand potential exposure in the community.
Read the radon.txt file

radon <- read.csv(here("data/radon.txt"))
head(radon)

  radon
1   3.8
2   1.7
3   5.5
4   2.1
5   1.6
6   6.5



(a) Draw a box plot of the radon concentrations
Draw a box plot of the radon concentrations and say whether the distribution is symmetrical or skewed. Your answer is the plot and your description.

ggplot(data = radon, mapping = aes(x = radon)) +
    coord_flip() +
    geom_boxplot()








Description: The distribution is skewed due to one outlier that is >30. Other than that, most values are less than or around 10.


(b) Calculate and report the average and median radon concentration

mean_radon <- mean(radon$radon)
median_radon <- median(radon$radon)
paste("Mean radon:  ", round(mean_radon, 2), "pCi/L")

[1] "Mean radon:   4.55 pCi/L"

paste("Median radon: ", round(median_radon, 2), "pCi/L")

[1] "Median radon:  3.5 pCi/L"




(c) Would you expect the average and median for these data to be similar?
No. Given the range of the data and the existence of an outlier away from the median, the mean will be pulled toward the outlier while the median will not.


(d) Calculate the standard error of the mean radon concentration

# SE = s / sqrt(n)
# calculate s (standard deviation)
s = sd(radon$radon)
# determine n (number of observations)
n = nrow(radon)
s / sqrt(n)

[1] 0.7556078


Imagine you have taken a second simple random sample of radon in Ramsey County, MN, homes. There are 250 homes in this sample.


(e) Would the second sample mean be close to the first sample?
Yes, since both are random samples from the same population and the first sample has sufficient observations (42), we can expect the mean of the second sample to be close to the first but we should also expect some sampling variability.


(f) Would the second sample standard error be close to that of the first?
No, the standard error SE is calculated as s / sqrt(n). Since the 2 samples are drawn randomly from the same population we can expect the standard deviation (s) to be close to that of the first sample but since the number of observations (n) in the 2nd sample are 250 vs 42 in the first, the SE for the 2nd sample will be lower.
The standard deviation of the first sample, s = 4.8968981 and se = sd(radon$radon) / sqrt(42) = 0.7556078
It is expected that the standard deviation remains close for both samples so the standard error for the 2nd sample se = sd(radon$radon) / sqrt(250) = 0.309707



Problem 3
Problem 3 (Mutagen effect): Scientists wanted to study whether a certain mutagen affects cell growth. They began with a large “master” cell culture and haphazardly took 9 vials from it. Four of these vials were randomly assigned to the control group (no mutagen), while the other five vials were assigned to the treatment group, where cells were exposed to 80 mg/ml dose of the mutagen. After giving the cells time to grow, the researchers examined them under a microscope. For each vial, they looked at 100 cells and counted how many showed microsatellite nuclei (tiny abnormalities that can signal mutations). The data (which are available in mutagen.csv) provide information about the treatment (no or dose) with the following values: - no: 0 dose (control): 0, 0, 0, 0 - dose: 80 mg/ml dose: 2, 3, 5, 11, 20
Answer the following questions based on these data.

(a) Design questions

What are the treatments in this study?

The treatments in the study are no treatment (Control group) or a treatment of an 80 mg/dl dose of the mutagen (Dose group)

What, if anything, are they randomly assigned to?

They are randomly assigned to vials of cell culture

Can causal conclusions be statistically justified? Why or why not?

The vials were randomly drawn from the cell culture and the treatments were randomly assigned to vials so yes, causal conclusions can be justified. But, the number of observations (9 vials) in the study are on the lower side so the conclusions could vary if a larger sample was used.
